newsitem.title: USA: U.S., China hail ties but problems remain.
newsitem.headline: U.S., China hail ties but problems remain.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen on Monday hailed positive momentum in bilateral ties, with Albright calling this a "pivotal year" for Sino-American relations.

But at the start of talks, Albright also stressed U.S. differences with China over human rights, Hong Kong and charges Beijing tried to influence last year's U.S. election campaign with political donations -- a charge she said is viewed "seriously" by Washington.
Qian appeared to reiterate Beijing's contention that it had no role in the alleged political contribution scandal, saying: "They (the charges) have nothing to do with China."

The two ministers, who met in February in Beijing, were to hold several hours of meetings, then a working dinner. They are preparing the way for a fall summit in Washington between President Bill Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin.
"For both America and China, the benefits of our dialogue are tangible and growing. We're not yet where we want to be but the direction in which we must go is clear," Albright said.
With the planned exchange of summits this year and next, "this is a pivotal year for U.S.-China relations," she said.

Qian was also upbeat, saying that "through the concerted efforts of both sides, Sino-U.S. relations have maintained the positive momentum of improvement and development" begun late last year after a long period of dangerous deterioration.

"Although there are some differences between China and the United States, they are far outnumbered by our common views to establish with the United States a long-term and stable friendly relationship," he added.

Albright and Qian were optimistic about prospects for an agreement on China's entry into the World Trade Organisation, maybe by the Clinton-Jiang summit. Demands that China improve market access have delayed Beijing's entry into the WTO.
"We are very hopeful that progress on these discussions will in fact be fruitful," Albright told a news conference with Qian before their meeting began.

Qian called recent WTO negotiations positive. Many complicated issues are involved but "both China and the United States share the common aspiration to resolve the question as soon as possible ... I believe that as time goes by these questions will be resolved," he said.

On the issue of renewing Most Favoured Nations trade benefits for China that some congressmen would like to withhold, Albright said: "We believe it is very important for the MFN to go forward ... It is a strategic imperative for this (U.S.-China) relationship to go forward and the trade relationship is very important in that regard."

Albright said she would stress in her talks U.S. concerns about China's human rights record as well as U.S. interest in China preserving a "high degree of autonomy and basic freedoms" in Hong Kong when the British colony reverts to Beijing's control on July 1.
She also said she would stress the U.S. expectation that differences between China and Taiwan, which Beijing considers a renegade province, be resolved peacefully.

Recent media reports that top Chinese officials may have approved attempts to influence U.S. elections through 1996 campaign donations has caused a furore and clouded the debate over renewing China's MFN trade status.
On this, Qian said: "I believe it's very usual for people to see political contributions and money politics in the United States. However they have nothing to do with China."
Albright noted that she raised the issue with Qian when she was in Beijing previously and "expressed to him how seriously we view these allegations. I will do so again."
She was expected to urge China to encourage North Korea to enter four-party peace talks. The effort stalled last week when Pyongyang tied its participation to more food aid.
Qian arrived just a week after United States hosted two prominent critics of Beijing: Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Martin Lee and the Dalai Lama, spiritual leader of Tibet.
The Chinese minister was to meet Defence Secretary William Cohen on Tuesday and Clinton on Wednesday.
